questions.q: In the absorption diagram, the structure labelled 'biological membrane' separates the:
opts: Intestinal lumen from the blood vessel lumen
Two lipid layers of the enterocyte
Carrier protein from the membrane pore
questions.exp: The diagram shows drug in the intestinal lumen crossing the biological membrane to reach the blood vessel lumen; every absorption mechanism (i-iv) is drawn across this membrane. (Book p2)

questions.q: In the legend of the absorption diagram, the Y-shaped symbol represents a:
questions.exp: The legend at the top of the diagram labels the Y-shaped symbol as 'carrier' and the triangle as 'drug'. (Book p2)

questions.q: In the legend of the absorption diagram, the triangle symbol represents:
questions.exp: The triangle is the symbol used throughout the diagram for the drug molecule, shown moving from intestinal lumen to blood vessel lumen. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which set lists the four mechanisms of absorption across the biological membrane in the order i to iv shown in the diagram?
opts: Filtration, simple/passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion, active transport
Simple diffusion, filtration, active transport, facilitated diffusion
Active transport, facilitated diffusion, filtration, simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion, active transport, filtration, simple diffusion
questions.exp: The diagram numbers the mechanisms i. Filtration, ii. Simple/passive diffusion (m/c), iii. Facilitated diffusion and iv. Active transport. (Book p2)

questions.q: The brace labelled 'ATP not required' in the absorption diagram covers which mechanisms?
opts: Filtration, simple/passive diffusion and facilitated diffusion
questions.exp: Filtration (i), simple/passive diffusion (ii) and facilitated diffusion (iii) are bracketed together as processes in which ATP is not required; only active transport needs ATP. (Book p2)

questions.q: Of the four absorption mechanisms shown, which one alone requires ATP?
questions.exp: Active transport (iv) is the only mechanism annotated 'ATP required'; the other three lie inside the 'ATP not required' brace. (Book p2)

questions.q: In the absorption diagram, the mechanism marked 'm/c' (most common) is:
questions.exp: Simple/passive diffusion carries the annotation 'm/c', i.e., it is the most common mechanism by which drugs cross biological membranes. (Book p2)

questions.q: In the absorption diagram, filtration (i) carries the drug across the membrane through:
questions.exp: Filtration is drawn as a drug moving through a pore/channel in the biological membrane, with no carrier involvement. (Book p2)

questions.q: The example of a drug absorbed by filtration given in the diagram is:
questions.exp: The diagram reads 'i. Filtration: Eg: Insulin (subcutaneous)' — insulin is the cited example of a drug absorbed through pores by filtration. (Book p2)

questions.q: Filtration as depicted in the absorption diagram requires which of the following?
opts: A concentration gradient but no ATP
questions.exp: Filtration sits under the 'ATP not required' brace: drug passes down its gradient through pores without ATP or a carrier. (Book p2)

questions.q: The most common mechanism of drug absorption across biological membranes is:
questions.exp: The diagram marks simple/passive diffusion as 'm/c' — the most common route of drug absorption. (Book p2)

questions.q: In the diagram, simple/passive diffusion (ii) is annotated as occurring:
opts: Against the concentration gradient using ATP
questions.exp: Simple/passive diffusion is labelled 'along conc. gradient' — the drug moves from higher to lower concentration without ATP. (Book p2)

questions.q: Filtration and simple/passive diffusion share which feature in the absorption diagram?
opts: Both occur along the concentration gradient
Both are independent of the concentration gradient
questions.exp: Filtration and simple diffusion both sit under 'ATP not required' and both move drug down its concentration gradient; only filtration uses membrane pores. (Book p2)

questions.q: Unlike simple/passive diffusion, filtration requires the drug to pass through:
questions.exp: Filtration is drawn as passage through a pore in the biological membrane, whereas simple diffusion is drawn crossing the membrane lipid directly. (Book p2)

questions.q: Mechanism iii, facilitated diffusion, differs from simple diffusion in that it requires:
questions.exp: The diagram draws facilitated diffusion with a carrier (it lies under the 'Carrier mediated transport' bracket) while still moving drug along the concentration gradient. (Book p2)

questions.q: The example of facilitated diffusion cited in the diagram is:
questions.exp: The diagram reads 'iii. Facilitated diffusion: Eg: GLUT receptors' — GLUT is the cited carrier for facilitated diffusion. (Book p2)

questions.q: GLUT-mediated absorption, as annotated in the diagram, is based on:
questions.exp: The annotation reads 'GLUT absorption based on gradient' — GLUT carriers move substrate down its concentration gradient without ATP. (Book p2)

questions.q: Does facilitated diffusion consume ATP?
opts: Yes, but only in the intestine
No, it lies under 'ATP not required'
Only when the gradient is reversed
questions.exp: Facilitated diffusion sits inside the brace marked 'ATP not required' in the diagram; it uses a carrier but no energy. (Book p2)

questions.q: Mechanism iv, active transport, is characterised in the diagram as:
opts: Along the concentration gradient, no ATP
Independent of concentration gradient and ATP
Independent of concentration gradient, ATP required
questions.exp: Active transport is annotated 'ATP required' and 'Independent of conc. gradient' — it can move drug irrespective of its concentration gradient. (Book p2)

questions.q: The example of active transport given in the diagram is:
questions.exp: The diagram reads 'iv. Active transport: ATP required. Eg: SGLT receptors'. (Book p2)

questions.q: According to the diagram, SGLT1 is located on the:
questions.exp: 'SGLT 1 → On small intestine.' is written under active transport in the absorption diagram. (Book p2)

questions.q: According to the diagram, SGLT2 is located on the:
questions.exp: 'SGLT 2 → On renal tubules.' is written under active transport in the absorption diagram. (Book p2)

questions.q: A drug is transported by SGLT1 in the small intestine. This is an example of:
questions.exp: SGLT receptors are the examples of active transport (iv), the ATP-requiring, carrier-mediated mechanism that is independent of the concentration gradient. (Book p2)

questions.q: The bracket labelled 'Carrier mediated transport' in the absorption diagram includes which mechanisms?
questions.exp: The carrier-mediated bracket encloses only mechanisms iii (facilitated diffusion) and iv (active transport). (Book p2)

questions.q: Which absorption mechanism can move a drug independent of its concentration gradient?
questions.exp: Only active transport (iv) is annotated 'independent of conc. gradient'; all the others move drug along the gradient. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which pair of mechanisms both use a carrier protein but differ in their ATP requirement?
questions.exp: Facilitated diffusion and active transport are both carrier mediated, but only active transport requires ATP — the key contrast of the diagram. (Book p2)

questions.q: The P-glycoprotein pump (Pgp) is also known as the:
questions.exp: The heading reads 'Active transport: P-glycoprotein pump (Pgp)/MDR1 pump' — Pgp and MDR1 are the same efflux pump. (Book p2)

questions.q: P-glycoprotein is described as the most common type of:
questions.exp: Below the heading the book notes 'm/c type of ABC pump' — Pgp is the most common ATP-binding cassette (ABC) pump. (Book p2)

questions.q: In the small intestine/liver diagram, most drugs cross the epithelial cell:
opts: Independent of the concentration gradient with ATP
By being effluxed back into the lumen
questions.exp: The diagram shows the upper arrow labelled 'Along the conc. gradient' ending in 'most drugs' — most drugs simply cross the epithelial cell down their gradient. (Book p3)

questions.q: In the same diagram, some drugs are pumped back out of the epithelial cell by the:
questions.exp: The lower arrow is driven by the green P-glycoprotein pump in the epithelial cell, which effluxes drug back into the intestinal lumen. (Book p3)

questions.q: Efflux of drug by Pgp in the small intestine results in:
questions.exp: The diagram links drug efflux to 'First pass metabolism — drug excreted before reaching systemic circulation'. (Book p3)

questions.q: As used in this diagram, first pass metabolism means the drug is:
opts: Metabolised by the liver after reaching systemic circulation
Excreted before reaching the systemic circulation
Converted to a prodrug in the gut wall
questions.exp: The diagram defines it explicitly: 'Drug excreted before reaching systemic circulation'. (Book p3)

questions.q: In the intestinal diagram, the drug effluxed by the Pgp pump is returned to the:
questions.exp: The efflux arrow points back from the epithelial cell into the intestinal lumen, so the drug never enters the blood vessel lumen. (Book p3)

questions.q: In the diagram, the Pgp pump is depicted on which side of the epithelial cell?
opts: The luminal border, returning drug to the intestinal lumen
The basolateral border, returning drug to blood
questions.exp: The green Pgp pump is drawn at the luminal border of the epithelial cell with its efflux arrow pointing back into the intestinal lumen. (Book p3)

questions.q: The book's stated significance of Pgp efflux is that the dosage of which drug is calculated from the amount lost?
questions.exp: 'Eg: Digoxin dosage is calculated based on amount being lost d/t drug efflux' — digoxin dosing must allow for the fraction effluxed by Pgp. (Book p3)

questions.q: Why must digoxin dosage be calculated on the amount lost to drug efflux?
opts: Because efflux converts digoxin to an active metabolite
Because part of the administered drug never reaches the systemic circulation
Because efflux increases digoxin's lipid solubility
Because efflux blocks digoxin's receptor binding
questions.exp: Pgp pumps digoxin back into the gut lumen so that fraction is excreted before reaching the systemic circulation; the dose is adjusted for this loss. (Book p3)

questions.q: According to the text, mdr1 pumps are present in the:
questions.exp: 'mdr1 pumps are present in BBB' — the BBB uses MDR1/Pgp to keep substrate drugs out of the CNS. (Book p3)

questions.q: Loperamide, the drug used as the BBB example, belongs to which class?
questions.exp: The text labels loperamide as '(opioid)' — it is an opioid that acts peripherally. (Book p3)

questions.q: The clinical use of loperamide stated in the text is:
questions.exp: 'Used in Rx: Diarrhoea' is written beside loperamide in the BBB diagram. (Book p3)

questions.q: Loperamide is described as acting on the:
questions.exp: 'Acts on GIT' — loperamide acts on the gastrointestinal tract, not on the central nervous system. (Book p3)

questions.q: Loperamide cannot cross the BBB because:
opts: mdr1 pumps in the BBB efflux it out
It is actively transported into the brain
It is too large a molecule
questions.exp: The diagram shows the mdr1 pump at the BBB returning loperamide back into blood, so it cannot enter the brain. (Book p3)

questions.q: The clinical consequence of loperamide being kept out of the brain by MDR1 pumps is that at usual doses it:
opts: Controls diarrhoea without central opioid effects
questions.exp: Because the BBB MDR1 pump excludes loperamide from the CNS, it acts on the GIT to control diarrhoea while producing no central opioid action. (Book p3)

questions.q: The note in the text mentions which other cause of drugs not crossing the BBB?
questions.exp: 'Note: Another cause of drugs not crossing BBB → water solubility' — polar, water-soluble drugs are repelled by the lipid BBB. (Book p3)

questions.q: Certain drugs cannot cross from the maternal circulation to the fetal circulation because of:
opts: Presence of MDR1 pumps in the placenta
Absence of pores in the placenta
questions.exp: The text states: 'Placenta: Certain drugs cannot cross from maternal circulation to fetal circulation d/t presence of MDR1 pumps in placenta.' (Book p3)

questions.q: Bile acid excretion, as described in the text, occurs due to:
opts: Presence of MDR1 pumps on hepatocytes
questions.exp: 'Bile acid excretion: D/t presence of MDR1 pumps on hepatocytes' — the same efflux pump handles biliary excretion. (Book p3)

questions.q: MDR1 pumps are described at all of the following sites EXCEPT the:
questions.exp: The text places MDR1 pumps at the BBB, the placenta and on hepatocytes (bile acid excretion); adipose tissue is not mentioned as an MDR1 site. (Book p3)

questions.q: In the flowchart for bacteria/tumour cells, the cell develops a Pgp pump which leads to:
questions.exp: The flowchart reads: Cell --develops--> Pgp pump --> Drug efflux --> Resistance. Efflux of the drug is what creates resistance. (Book p3)

questions.q: According to that flowchart, resistance in bacteria and tumour cells is the end-result of:
opts: Drug efflux by the Pgp pump
Enhanced metabolic activation of the drug
questions.exp: The sequence ends 'Drug efflux → Resistance', i.e., the pump expels the drug and the cell survives as resistant. (Book p3)

questions.q: The first step of the resistance flowchart is that the cell:
questions.exp: The flowchart begins 'Cell —develops→ Pgp pump', which is then followed by drug efflux and resistance. (Book p3)

questions.q: Under 'Pharmacological significance', the three categories of drugs related to the Pgp pump are:
questions.exp: The page branches into three columns: Substrate (undergoes efflux by pump), Inducers (increase number of pumps) and Inhibitors (decrease number of pumps). (Book p4)

questions.q: A Pgp 'substrate' is defined in the chart as a drug that:
questions.exp: The substrate column reads 'undergoes efflux by pump' and lists loperamide, cyclosporine and digoxin. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a Pgp substrate?
questions.exp: Loperamide heads the substrate list. Rifampicin and phenytoin are inducers and verapamil is an inhibitor, so they efflux poorly but modify the pump instead. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which set lists the Pgp substrates given in the chart?
questions.exp: The substrate column lists loperamide, cyclosporine and digoxin — the drugs that are pumped out by Pgp. (Book p4)

questions.q: Pgp inducers act by increasing the number of pumps, which causes:
questions.exp: The inducer column reads '↑ no. of pump (Causes drug failure)' — more efflux lowers drug levels and the drug fails. (Book p4)

questions.q: The inducer column equates Pgp inducers with:
questions.exp: '≈ Enzyme inducers' — the same drugs that induce hepatic enzymes (rifampicin, phenytoin, phenobarbital) also induce Pgp. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a Pgp inducer?
questions.exp: The inducers are rifampicin, phenytoin and phenobarbital; verapamil, quinidine and neratinib appear in the inhibitor column. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which set lists the Pgp inducers given in the chart?
questions.exp: The inducer column lists rifampicin, phenytoin and phenobarbital — the classic enzyme inducers, which also increase Pgp number. (Book p4)

questions.q: Pgp inhibitors decrease the number of pumps, which causes:
questions.exp: The inhibitor column reads '↓ no. of pumps (Causes drug toxicity)' — less efflux means drug accumulates to toxic levels. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a Pgp inhibitor?
questions.exp: Itraconazole is in the inhibitor list; rifampicin, phenobarbital and phenytoin are inducers, so they act in the opposite direction. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which drug appears in BOTH the substrate and the inhibitor lists of the chart?
questions.exp: Cyclosporine is listed both as a substrate (undergoes efflux) and as an inhibitor (decreases pump number) — an important dual role. (Book p4)

questions.q: Erythromycin/clarithromycin appear in the chart under which category?
questions.exp: The last entry of the inhibitor column is 'Erythromycin/Clarithromycin', i.e., these macrolides inhibit Pgp and thereby cause drug toxicity. (Book p4)

questions.q: As per the 'Effects of blockade' table, blockage by rifampicin results in:
questions.exp: The table pairs rifampicin with 'Digoxin failure' — rifampicin reduces effective digoxin availability, so digoxin fails. (Book p4)

questions.q: As per the table, which drug's blockade of Pgp causes digoxin toxicity?
questions.exp: The table pairs clarithromycin with 'Digoxin toxicity' — inhibiting Pgp lets digoxin accumulate to toxic levels. (Book p4)

questions.q: As per the table, cyclosporine's effect through Pgp blockade is:
questions.exp: The table pairs cyclosporine with 'Cholestatic jaundice' — retention of bile acids/acids due to blocked hepatic efflux explains the jaundice. (Book p4)

questions.q: As per the table, verapamil's Pgp blockade is used for:
opts: Reversal of drug resistance in cancer and bacteria
questions.exp: The table reads 'verapamil — used in reversal of drug resistance (Cancer, bacteria)': blocking the efflux pump restores drug accumulation in resistant cells. (Book p4)

questions.q: As per the table, quinidine's Pgp blockade produces:
questions.exp: The last row pairs quinidine with 'Loperamide induced central S/E' — with Pgp blocked, loperamide is no longer excluded from the CNS. (Book p4)

questions.q: A patient on digoxin is started on clarithromycin and develops digoxin toxicity. The mechanism is:
opts: Induction of Pgp increasing digoxin efflux
Blockade of Pgp reducing digoxin efflux
Displacement of digoxin from plasma proteins
Increased renal tubular secretion of digoxin
questions.exp: Clarithromycin blocks Pgp; with less efflux, digoxin accumulates and toxicity results — exactly as the table records 'Clarithromycin → Digoxin toxicity'. (Book p4)

questions.q: A patient on digoxin is started on rifampicin and her digoxin effect is lost. As per the table this is:
opts: Digoxin failure from the rifampicin-Pgp interaction
questions.exp: The table lists 'Rifampicin → Digoxin failure'; rifampicin increases Pgp-mediated digoxin efflux, so the digoxin level and effect fall. (Book p4)

questions.q: Verapamil's Pgp-blocking property is exploited in which two settings, as stated in the table?
questions.exp: The table specifies reversal of drug resistance in cancer and bacteria — resistant cells re-accumulate the cytotoxic/antibiotic drug when the efflux pump is blocked. (Book p4)

questions.q: A patient taking loperamide for diarrhoea is given quinidine and develops central opioid side effects. The explanation is that quinidine:
opts: Blocks the BBB Pgp pump, allowing loperamide into the CNS
questions.exp: Normally MDR1 pumps at the BBB exclude loperamide; quinidine blocks Pgp, so loperamide enters the brain and gives central side effects — as tabulated under quinidine. (Book p4)

questions.q: In the passive diffusion diagram, the two vertical lines labelled 'Lipid' represent:
opts: Lipid membranes the drug must cross
questions.exp: The diagram draws drug in the intestinal lumen facing two lipid layers, labelled 'Lipid', between which the charged membrane proteins sit. (Book p4)

questions.q: In the passive diffusion diagram, the ellipse labelled 'Proteins charged' indicates that the membrane proteins:
questions.exp: The charged membrane proteins are the reason a polar, ionised or charged molecule is 'Repelled' and not absorbed. (Book p4)

questions.q: In the passive diffusion diagram, a polar/ionised/charged drug is shown to be:
questions.exp: The upper arrow carries the label 'Repelled' back into the intestinal lumen — charged molecules cannot cross the lipid membrane by passive diffusion. (Book p4)

questions.q: According to the passive diffusion diagram, the fate of a polar/ionised, water-soluble drug is that it is:
questions.exp: The diagram states: 'Polar/ionised/charged — water soluble: excreted' and 'Not absorbed (Lipid insoluble/water soluble)'. (Book p4)

questions.q: In the passive diffusion diagram, a non-polar/unionised/neutral drug is:
questions.exp: The lower arrow of the diagram ends in 'Absorbed (Lipid soluble)' — unionised, non-polar molecules diffuse across the lipid membrane. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which property of the membrane explains why ionised drugs are not passively absorbed?
opts: Its charged membrane proteins repel charged molecules
Its pores are too small for any ion
Its carriers only accept unionised drugs
Its inner lipid layer is water soluble
questions.exp: The proteins embedded in the lipid membranes are annotated 'charged', so polar/ionised/charged drugs are repelled rather than crossing. (Book p4)

questions.q: Drugs described in the diagram as 'lipid insoluble/water soluble' are:
questions.exp: The diagram equates lipid-insoluble/water-soluble character with 'Not absorbed' during passive diffusion. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which of these drugs would be best absorbed by passive diffusion?
opts: A polar drug with a high charge density
questions.exp: Passive diffusion requires a non-polar/unionised/neutral molecule that is lipid soluble; charged or water-soluble drugs are repelled and excreted. (Book p4)

units.title: Four Ways Across the Biological Membrane
units.guide: A drug in the intestinal lumen must cross the biological membrane to reach blood. The diagram draws four mechanisms — filtration, simple/passive diffusion (the most common), facilitated diffusion and active transport — with the first three bracketed as ATP-independent and only active transport needing ATP. The legend uses a Y for carrier and a triangle for drug.

units.title: Filtration & Simple Diffusion: The ATP-Free Routes
units.guide: Filtration pushes the drug through membrane pores (example: subcutaneous insulin) with no ATP; simple/passive diffusion is the commonest mechanism of absorption and moves drug along its concentration gradient, straight through the lipid membrane rather than a pore. Neither uses a carrier and neither burns ATP.

units.title: Facilitated Diffusion vs Active Transport
units.guide: Facilitated diffusion (GLUT receptors) uses a carrier but still runs along the gradient with no ATP, and GLUT absorption is gradient-based. Active transport (SGLT receptors) needs ATP and is independent of the gradient — SGLT1 sits on the small intestine and SGLT2 on the renal tubules. Together these two form 'carrier mediated transport'.

units.title: P-glycoprotein (MDR1) Pump & First-Pass Efflux
units.guide: P-glycoprotein — the most common ABC pump, also called MDR1 — is an ATP-driven efflux pump. In the small intestine/liver most drugs cross the epithelial cell along the concentration gradient, but some are pumped back into the intestinal lumen, producing first-pass metabolism: the drug is excreted before it ever reaches the systemic circulation.

units.title: Digoxin Dosing, BBB, Placenta & Hepatocytes
units.guide: Efflux matters clinically: digoxin dosage is calculated on the amount lost to efflux. MDR1 pumps sit at the blood-brain barrier, so the opioid antidiarrhoeal loperamide acts on the GIT but cannot enter the brain; water solubility is another reason drugs stay out of the CNS. Placental MDR1 pumps protect the fetus, and hepatocyte MDR1 pumps drive bile acid excretion.

units.title: Pgp-Driven Resistance in Bacteria & Tumour Cells
units.guide: The flowchart is short and ruthless: a bacterial or tumour cell develops a Pgp pump, the pump effluxes the drug, and the cell becomes resistant — the same pump that handles normal drugs becomes the engine of treatment failure.

units.title: Substrates, Inducers & Inhibitors of Pgp
units.guide: Three columns summarise Pgp pharmacology: substrates (loperamide, cyclosporine, digoxin) are pumped out; inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, phenobarbital — like enzyme inducers) raise pump numbers and cause drug failure; inhibitors (verapamil, amiodarone, quinidine, cyclosporine, itraconazole, neratinib, erythromycin/clarithromycin) lower pump numbers and cause drug toxicity. Cyclosporine is both substrate and inhibitor.

units.title: Effects of Pgp Blockade: The Interaction Table
units.guide: The blockade table is pure exam gold: rifampicin → digoxin failure, clarithromycin → digoxin toxicity, cyclosporine → cholestatic jaundice, verapamil → reversal of drug resistance in cancer and bacteria, and quinidine → loperamide-induced central side effects. Each entry is a clinical interaction driven by the efflux pump.

units.title: Passive Diffusion: The Lipid-Solubility Rule
units.guide: Passive diffusion obeys one rule: lipid-soluble wins. A non-polar, unionised, neutral drug diffuses across the lipid membrane and is absorbed; a polar, ionised or charged drug is repelled by the charged membrane proteins, is lipid insoluble/water soluble, is not absorbed and is finally excreted.
